headline: Cyclosporiasis — Lucas County at 1,226 as of August 4; under 10 new cases per day; primary outbreak functionally concluded; second unnamed cluster remains open
paragraphs: The Toledo-Lucas County Health Department confirmed on June 30 the first cases of cyclosporiasis — a diarrheal intestinal illness caused by the parasite Cyclospora cayetanensis — in Lucas County residents, marking the Toledo metro's entry into an outbreak spreading across northwest Ohio and southeast Michigan. By July 8, Lucas County was leading all Ohio counties in confirmed cases; The Blade reported at least 65 Lucas County residents ill as of July 1, with case counts climbing steadily into early July. The Ohio Department of Health (ODH) issued a formal advisory on July 8, with ODH Director Dr. Keith Vanderhoff urging precautions and noting cyclosporiasis requires antibiotic treatment not resolved by over-the-counter antidiarrheal medications. CNBC reported July 13 that the national outbreak has surpassed 1,000 confirmed cases, with the Midwest — and northwest Ohio in particular — disproportionately represented. NW Ohio total cases exceeded 600 as of mid-July.

No specific food item or venue has been publicly identified as the source of the Lucas County outbreak as of this brief. The Toledo-Lucas County Health Department, Monroe County Health Department in Michigan, Ohio Department of Health, and federal agencies are jointly investigating, with patient interviews focused on grocery and dining locations in the 2–14 days before symptom onset. Past national cyclosporiasis outbreaks have been linked to contaminated fresh produce. Symptoms include watery diarrhea, stomach cramping, bloating, fatigue, and nausea; onset typically follows ingestion by 2 to 14 days. The Toledo-Lucas County Health Department has published updated case counts and guidance at lucascountyhealth.com/cyclo.

As of July 14-15, the 2026 outbreak has become the worst year on record for U.S. cyclosporiasis, surpassing the prior record of approximately 4,700 confirmed cases set in 2019. Cases have been confirmed in at least 31 states. Michigan's chief medical executive Dr. Natasha Bagdasarian said data from more than 1,000 patient interviews consistently implicates lettuce or salad greens as the exposure vehicle. Taco Bell has emerged as a focus of the traceback investigation: the Washington Post reported July 14 that authorities are actively investigating Taco Bell and lettuce as the outbreak source. Yum Brands confirmed to CNBC that Taco Bell voluntarily pulled select produce items — including lettuce, guacamole, pico de gallo, and cilantro onion — at select Detroit-area locations. Taco Bell stated there is 'no confirmed link' to the outbreak; no FDA recall has been issued naming the chain as of this brief. The CDC's official outbreak page continues to list the food source as 'unknown.' No specific Toledo restaurant or grocery supplier has been named in connection with the Lucas County case cluster.

As of July 15-16, northwest Ohio confirmed cases reached 1,199 — up 80 in a single day from July 14's count of 1,119, per The Blade's July 15 reporting. Lucas County's confirmed case total reached 682, rising from 531 on July 13 to 638 on July 14 and 682 on July 15, according to the Toledo-Lucas County Health Department's newly launched public dashboard at lucascountyhealth.com/cyclo, which updates weekday case counts at approximately noon. The Blade reported July 14 that northwest Ohio had officially exceeded 1,000 confirmed cases — a regional milestone. Wood County health officials also announced a local case tally, extending the outbreak's confirmed geographic reach within northwest Ohio. Nationally, NBC News reported that the CDC now counts nearly 7,000 suspected cases — 1,645 laboratory-confirmed plus approximately 5,100 under investigation — roughly 1.5 times the prior U.S. record of 4,700. No FDA recall has been issued as of this brief; the CDC's outbreak page continues to list the food source as 'unknown'; no Toledo restaurant or grocery supplier has been named. The Glass City JazzFest at Glass City Metropark is now fewer than 30 days away.

On July 16, federal investigators publicly identified the outbreak source for the first time. The CDC and FDA linked the outbreak to shredded iceberg lettuce supplied by Taylor Farms — a large California-based agricultural company — to Taco Bell restaurants in five states: Indiana, Kentucky, Michigan, Ohio, and West Virginia. The Washington Post, CNN, and Bloomberg Law all reported July 16 that investigators had traced contaminated lettuce to a single supplier shipping from Mexico. Taco Bell announced it is removing lettuce from its U.S. locations nationwide indefinitely and will replace it with lettuce from alternative sources; notices at some Detroit-area Taco Bell restaurants had already informed customers the chain was 'currently unable to sell' lettuce, pico de gallo, guacamole, and cilantro onion. No FDA recall has been issued as of this brief — investigators describe Taylor Farms lettuce as a 'potential source' rather than a confirmed causal link; the CDC's official outbreak page updated its title to 'Cyclospora Outbreak Linked to Shredded Iceberg Lettuce Served at Taco Bell in 5 States.' Michigan's case total has surpassed 4,300 — with at least 100 hospitalizations — concentrated in southeast Michigan, where the Detroit metro carries the heaviest case load. NW Ohio cases reached 1,409 as of The Blade's July 16 reporting, with Lucas County at 750 — both up significantly from the July 15 count of 1,199 and 682, respectively. Nationally, 141 hospitalizations and nearly 7,000 confirmed or under-investigation cases have been recorded.

On July 17, Taylor Farms de Mexico formally announced a voluntary recall of all iceberg lettuce sourced from central Mexico — the first official recall of the 2026 outbreak. The FDA simultaneously published a formal advisory: 'Do not eat shredded iceberg lettuce from Mexico served at Taco Bell locations in Indiana, Kentucky, Michigan, Ohio, and West Virginia.' Taylor Farms stated the recall was prompted by information provided by the FDA. Taco Bell confirmed it 'has completed removal of affected Taylor Farms lettuce from our restaurants' and that 'the affected ingredient has been removed from our supply chain nationwide.' The Ohio Department of Health reported July 17 that Ohio has reached 1,316 confirmed cyclosporiasis cases — the state total topping 1,000 for the first time — with 96 hospitalizations statewide. ODH's confirmed count for Lucas County stands at 278. That figure is substantially lower than the 750 reported by the Toledo-Lucas County Health Department's dashboard at lucascountyhealth.com/cyclo, which tracks all reported and pending laboratory cases including those under investigation; the ODH figure reflects only lab-confirmed results in its system. The Toledo-Lucas County Health Department separately launched a survey — administered through the Ohio Department of Health — for any Lucas County resident who has tested positive for cyclosporiasis, to aid the investigation. With the supply chain exposure severed by Taco Bell's nationwide lettuce removal and the Taylor Farms recall, public health officials expect the incubation period (2–14 days) to determine when new cases stop appearing; any new cases arising after July 17 would reflect exposures prior to the recall.

Also on July 17, Michigan's cyclosporiasis case total surpassed 5,000 — up from 4,312 on July 16 — according to the Detroit News, making Michigan the most heavily affected state in the 2026 outbreak. Cases remain concentrated in southeast Michigan. July 19 is day two of the post-recall surveillance window. The Toledo-Lucas County Health Department's dashboard at lucascountyhealth.com/cyclo updates weekdays at approximately noon; no new case count is expected until Monday, July 20. The last published Lucas County total stands at 750 (NW Ohio: 1,409) as of July 16. Public health officials expect Cyclospora's 2–14-day incubation window to govern when new-exposure cases stop appearing; any case arising after July 17 reflects exposure prior to the recall. The Glass City JazzFest at Glass City Metropark is now 27 days away (August 15).

July 20 marks day three of the post-recall surveillance window and the first scheduled weekday case-count update from the Toledo-Lucas County Health Department's dashboard at lucascountyhealth.com/cyclo since the Taylor Farms voluntary recall was announced July 17. The dashboard updates at approximately noon on weekdays; as of this brief's publication, no confirmed updated count had appeared in available sources — the last published figures stand at Lucas County: 750 and NW Ohio: 1,409, as of July 16. Epidemiologists note that Cyclospora's 2–14-day incubation period means cases appearing this week may still reflect exposures predating the July 17 supply chain severance; a meaningful deceleration in daily new cases — if it materializes in today's and subsequent dashboard updates — will be the earliest empirical signal that removing Taylor Farms lettuce from Taco Bell's supply chain is working. The Glass City JazzFest at Glass City Metropark is now 26 days away (August 15).

Northwest Ohio surpassed 2,000 cyclosporiasis cases over the weekend. The Blade reported July 20 that the regional total reached 2,029 — up from 1,673 on Friday, July 17, the same day the Taylor Farms recall was announced — with Lucas County's confirmed case count rising to 967, up from 750 on July 16. The continued surge in weekend case counts confirms that Cyclospora's 2–14-day incubation period is masking any near-term signal from the supply chain intervention: cases appearing this week still reflect exposures prior to the July 17 recall. A meaningful plateau or deceleration signal is not expected until late July at the earliest.

On July 20, the FDA disclosed a significant complication in the investigation: the laboratory sample of Taylor Farms lettuce that tested positive for Cyclospora — the physical evidence cited when investigators linked the outbreak to Taylor Farms de Mexico and prompted the July 17 voluntary recall — was a false positive. CNBC, NBC News, and the Washington Post all reported the FDA's finding; the agency stated that 'due to the complexity in detection of Cyclospora, FDA laboratory experts re-reviewed the sample results and have concluded that the finding does not represent true amplification and should be considered a false positive.' As of the FDA's July 20 statement, there are no confirmed positive laboratory samples linking Taylor Farms lettuce to Cyclospora. Crucially, the Taylor Farms voluntary recall remains in effect: Taylor Fresh Foods said the recall was kept in place 'out of an abundance of caution.' The FDA has not reversed its conclusion that Taylor Farms is linked to the outbreak — the epidemiological case (patient interview data consistently pointing to Taco Bell lettuce) stands even without a confirmed laboratory sample. The false positive means the physical evidence underpinning the recall has been retracted; the investigation continues on epidemiological grounds alone.

On July 21 — day five of the post-recall surveillance window — The Blade reported that cyclosporiasis cases continue to rise in northwest Ohio, consistent with Cyclospora's 2–14-day incubation period: new cases appearing this week still reflect exposures prior to the July 17 Taylor Farms recall. The Toledo-Lucas County Health Department's dashboard at lucascountyhealth.com/cyclo updated at approximately noon on July 21, its regular weekday cadence. The dashboard tracks all reported and pending laboratory cases, including those under investigation; the Ohio Department of Health's confirmed-laboratory-only figure continues to lag. A meaningful signal of deceleration remains expected no earlier than late July.

On July 22 — day six of the post-recall surveillance window — The Blade confirmed northwest Ohio cyclosporiasis cases have topped 2,200. The Toledo-Lucas County Health Department's dashboard recorded 2,268 NW Ohio cases and 1,044 Lucas County cases, up from 2,029 NW Ohio and 967 Lucas County as of July 20. The continued surge is within the expected epidemiological range: Cyclospora's incubation period spans 2–14 days, meaning exposures occurring on July 17 — the day of the recall — could produce confirmed cases through July 31. Epidemiologists are watching for a sustained deceleration in the daily rate-of-change as the first empirical signal that removing Taylor Farms lettuce from Taco Bell's supply chain is working. The Glass City JazzFest at Glass City Metropark is now 23 days away (August 15).

On July 23 — day seven of the post-recall surveillance window — The Blade reported northwest Ohio cyclosporiasis cases reached 2,380 and Lucas County cases reached 1,074, up from 2,268 and 1,044 as of July 22. The continued climb remains within epidemiological expectations: new cases this week still reflect exposures before the July 17 Taylor Farms recall. The Toledo-Lucas County Health Department launched a public information hotline — 419-213-2884, Monday through Friday, 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. — as resident inquiries surged; voicemail is available for after-hours callback. The Glass City JazzFest at Glass City Metropark is 22 days away (August 15).

Also on July 23, the Ohio Department of Health formally requested federal assistance, and the CDC confirmed it will deploy a team of epidemiologists — referred to as 'disease detectives' — to Ohio for approximately three weeks to conduct in-person interviews of confirmed cases, analyze exposure histories, and identify common exposure locations and foods. A significant new development emerged from the national investigation: the FDA disclosed a second cluster of 72 cyclosporiasis cases linked to a food product that has not yet been publicly identified, separate from the Taylor Farms iceberg lettuce implicated in the five-state Taco Bell outbreak. The emergence of a second, unnamed source indicates the 2026 outbreak may have a more complex exposure landscape than a single recall can address. Michigan and Ohio together account for more than 9,000 cases; nationally, the CDC has confirmed 4,173 laboratory cases and is investigating more than 7,400 additional suspected cases.

On July 24 — day eight of the post-recall surveillance window — The Blade reported northwest Ohio cyclosporiasis cases reached 2,508 and Lucas County cases reached 1,113, reflecting a net increase of approximately 479 regional cases over the preceding week. The Ohio Department of Health recorded 2,596 statewide confirmed cases as of July 24. No deceleration signal is visible in the case counts: Cyclospora's 2–14-day incubation period means exposures occurring on or before July 17 — the day of the Taylor Farms voluntary recall — could produce confirmed cases through July 31. Fox 19 reported that CDC disease detectives are now actively conducting field interviews with confirmed Ohio cases to analyze exposure histories and identify common exposure locations. Lucas County's count (1,113 cases) remains the highest of any Ohio county. Today is Saturday, July 25; no TLCHD dashboard update is expected until Monday, when the next weekday posting will reflect weekend accumulation. A meaningful deceleration in the daily rate-of-change remains the primary metric to watch in next week's updates.

Monday, July 27 — day 10 of the post-recall surveillance window — is the first scheduled weekday case-count update from the Toledo-Lucas County Health Department's dashboard at lucascountyhealth.com/cyclo since the July 24 posting. The dashboard updates at approximately noon on weekdays; as of this brief's publication, the July 27 update had not yet appeared in available sources — the last published figures remain Lucas County: 1,113 and NW Ohio: 2,508, as of July 24. Cyclospora's 2–14-day incubation period means exposures occurring on July 17 — the day of the Taylor Farms voluntary recall — could produce confirmed cases through July 31; a meaningful deceleration in the daily rate-of-change before that date would be the first empirical signal that removing Taylor Farms lettuce from Taco Bell's supply chain is working. Separately, the FDA has confirmed a second distinct cluster of 72 cyclosporiasis cases under active investigation; the food vehicle has not been publicly identified — CBS News reported the source has not been specified. For Toledo's summer calendar: Jeep Fest (August 6–9, 100K+ attendees) is now 10 days away and Glass City JazzFest (August 15, free outdoor event) is 19 days away; neither has announced health-related changes.

On July 27 — day 10 of the post-recall window — The Blade reported 180 new cyclosporiasis cases over the preceding weekend (July 25–26), bringing northwest Ohio's cumulative total to 2,689 and Lucas County's confirmed case count to 1,149. This is the first potential deceleration signal in the outbreak's trajectory. For context: the prior week (July 17–24) added approximately 479 new NW Ohio cases across seven days, an average of roughly 68 per day; the weekend increment of 180 cases across two days works out to approximately 90 per day — a modest arithmetic decline, but the first sustained lower-rate count since the outbreak began its rapid climb in mid-July. Cyclospora's maximum 14-day incubation period means any exposure occurring on July 17 — the day of the Taylor Farms voluntary recall — could produce a confirmed case no later than July 31. Cases appearing after July 31 would reflect either the unresolved second unnamed cluster (72 cases, food vehicle unknown) or ongoing secondary transmission. The July 28 TLCHD dashboard update — the first Tuesday posting after the July 27 weekend accumulation figure — is the next key data point.

On July 28 — day 12 of the post-recall surveillance window — The Blade reported 96 new cyclosporiasis cases in northwest Ohio, bringing the regional cumulative total to 2,785 and Lucas County's confirmed case count to 1,173 (up 24 in one day). The July 28 single-day count of 96 new NW Ohio cases is consistent with continued deceleration: for comparison, the week of July 17–24 added approximately 479 regional cases across seven days (~68/day), and the prior Tuesday-to-Tuesday single-day comparison yielded larger daily increments. The deceleration trajectory is now visible across three consecutive data points (July 24 → July 27 weekend → July 28), though case counts remain elevated. July 31 is the hard epidemiological boundary: under Cyclospora's maximum 14-day incubation period, no case arising after July 31 can reflect an exposure on or before July 17 — the day of the Taylor Farms voluntary recall. New cases reported after July 31 would reflect either the unresolved second unnamed cluster (72 cases, food vehicle unknown, active FDA investigation) or another exposure source not yet identified. CDC disease detectives remain in Ohio conducting field interviews. For Toledo's summer calendar: Jeep Fest (August 6–9, 100K+ attendees) is 8 days away and Glass City JazzFest (August 15, free outdoor event) is 17 days away; neither has announced health-related changes.

On July 29 — day 13 of the post-recall surveillance window — The Blade reported only 10 new cyclosporiasis cases in Lucas County, bringing the county's confirmed case count to 1,183, while northwest Ohio reached 2,856 total cases (up 71 from July 28's 2,785). Michigan's confirmed case total surpassed 10,000; Bloomberg reported the milestone July 29, with cases remaining concentrated in the southeast Michigan metro. The 10-case single-day Lucas County increment is the most dramatic deceleration signal yet in the outbreak: Lucas County added 24 cases on July 28, and mid-July single-day peaks exceeded 80. Today (July 30) is the TLCHD dashboard's scheduled noon update — Day 14 of the post-recall window and the penultimate weekday posting before July 31, the hard epidemiological boundary. Under Cyclospora's maximum 14-day incubation period, no case arising after July 31 can reflect a Taylor Farms exposure from July 17. If the Lucas County daily increment holds in the single digits or teens through today's and tomorrow's updates, the primary outbreak will be functionally contained. New cases reported on or after August 1 would reflect either the unresolved second unnamed cluster (72 cases, food vehicle unknown, active FDA investigation) or another unidentified exposure source. CDC disease detectives remain in Ohio conducting field interviews. Jeep Fest (August 6–9, 100K+ attendees) is now 7 days away; Glass City JazzFest (August 15, free outdoor event) is 16 days away; neither has announced health-related changes.

On July 30 — Day 14 of the post-recall surveillance window and the final weekday update before the epidemiological boundary — The Blade reported 11 new cyclosporiasis cases in Lucas County, bringing the county's confirmed case count to 1,194, while northwest Ohio reached 2,926 total cases (up 70 from July 29's 2,856). The 11-case Lucas County daily increment is consistent with the sustained deceleration trajectory: Lucas County added 24 on July 28, 10 on July 29, and 11 on July 30 — the smallest three-day rolling average since the outbreak's mid-July peak, when single-day county increments exceeded 80. Today, July 31, is the hard epidemiological boundary: under Cyclospora's maximum 14-day incubation period, any case produced by a July 17 Taylor Farms exposure must appear no later than today. The TLCHD dashboard at lucascountyhealth.com/cyclo is scheduled to post its noon weekday update; that figure is the definitive test of whether the primary outbreak is functionally contained. Cases reported on or after August 1 will reflect either the unresolved second unnamed cluster (72 cases, food vehicle unknown, active FDA investigation) or another unidentified exposure source. Nationally, the 2026 outbreak has surpassed 18,000 confirmed or suspected cases in 41 states with 423 hospitalizations — the worst Cyclospora outbreak in U.S. history. CDC disease detectives remain in Ohio conducting field interviews. Jeep Fest (August 6–9, 100K+ attendees) is now 6 days away; Glass City JazzFest (August 14–15, dual-venue event) is 14 days away; neither has announced health-related changes.

On July 31 — the hard epidemiological boundary — The Blade reported 13 new cyclosporiasis cases in Lucas County, bringing the county's confirmed total to 1,207, while northwest Ohio reached 3,016 total cases (up 90 from July 30's 2,926). The Ohio Department of Health recorded 4,013 statewide confirmed cases as of July 31, per WOSU. Lucas County's 13-case July 31 increment continues the sustained deceleration from mid-July daily peaks exceeding 80; the broader northwest Ohio uptick (+90 vs. +70 on July 30) indicates surrounding counties are still accumulating cases even as the Lucas County epicenter slows. Today, August 1, is the first post-boundary day: under Cyclospora's maximum 14-day incubation period, no case arising on or after today can reflect a July 17 Taylor Farms exposure. Any new case count published at today's TLCHD noon update — and all subsequent daily figures — reflects either the second unnamed cluster (which has grown from 72 to at least 93 cases, food vehicle still unidentified by FDA) or another exposure source not yet identified. Two additional national developments: the Taylor Farms/Taco Bell outbreak has expanded from the original 5 states to 9 states (Michigan, Ohio, Indiana, Kentucky, West Virginia, Illinois, Oklahoma, Kansas, and Pennsylvania); the FDA is running at least six active Cyclospora outbreak investigations simultaneously. Toledo's summer calendar: Jeep Fest (August 6–9, 100K+ attendees) is 5 days away and Glass City JazzFest (August 14–15, dual-venue event) is 13 days away; neither has announced health-related changes.

August 1 (Saturday) and August 2 (Sunday) are non-publishing days for the Toledo-Lucas County Health Department's cyclosporiasis dashboard at lucascountyhealth.com/cyclo, which updates weekdays at approximately noon. No case-count update is expected until Monday, August 3 — the first scheduled weekday posting in the post-boundary window. That figure will be the first empirical data point for whether any new cases are accumulating absent the Taylor Farms exposure pathway; any cases reported on August 3 or later will reflect either the second unnamed cluster (now 93+ cases, food vehicle still unidentified by FDA, active investigation ongoing) or another exposure source not yet identified. The last published TLCHD figures stand at Lucas County: 1,207 and Northwest Ohio: 3,016 as of July 31. Jeep Fest (August 6–9, 100K+ attendees) begins in four days and Glass City JazzFest (August 14–15) is 12 days away; both event organizers have maintained no health-related changes.

Monday, August 3 is the first scheduled weekday post-boundary update from the Toledo-Lucas County Health Department's cyclosporiasis dashboard. The dashboard updates at approximately noon; as of this brief, the August 3 noon figure is pending. The last published counts remain Lucas County: 1,207 and NW Ohio: 3,016 as of July 31 — figures from the final day of the primary outbreak window. Any case count appearing in today's or subsequent TLCHD updates reflects only the second unnamed cluster (93+ cases, food vehicle still unidentified by FDA, active investigation ongoing under at least six parallel FDA Cyclospora probes) or another unidentified exposure source. If today's Lucas County increment is in the single digits or zero, the primary Taco Bell/Taylor Farms outbreak will be empirically confirmed as functionally concluded for the region. CDC disease detectives remain in Ohio conducting field interviews. Toledo Jeep Fest (August 6–9, 100,000+ attendees) opens in three days and Glass City JazzFest (August 14–15) is 11 days out; neither event has announced health-related changes.

The August 3 TLCHD noon dashboard update confirmed the deceleration trajectory: only 11 new cases were recorded over the July 31–August 3 weekend, bringing Lucas County's cumulative confirmed case total to 1,218 and northwest Ohio to 3,094. WTOL reported Lucas County cases are 'leveling off'; 13abc reported cases 'trending down.' For context, the peak of the local outbreak was the week of July 5–11, when 443 positive lab tests were collected in Lucas County; by the final week of July heading into August, that weekly rate had fallen to 37. The 11-case weekend increment is consistent with post-boundary surveillance of the second unnamed cluster (now 93+ cases, food vehicle still unidentified by FDA) rather than any residual Taylor Farms exposure pathway. Separately, Michigan reported its first two cyclosporiasis deaths on August 3 — the first deaths attributed to the 2026 outbreak. CNBC, NBC News, CNN, ClickOnDetroit, and 13abc all confirmed the deaths; officials noted both individuals had significant underlying health conditions. Michigan's case total stands at more than 11,000 — concentrated in southeast Michigan — with 193 hospitalizations. Deaths from cyclosporiasis are rare in the United States; Lucas County health officials emphasized the illness is not life-threatening for most patients.

The Toledo-Lucas County Health Department's dashboard at lucascountyhealth.com/cyclo recorded 1,226 Lucas County confirmed cases and 3,119 northwest Ohio total cases as of the August 4 noon weekday update — an increment of 8 new Lucas County cases since August 3. The Blade published 'New cyclosporiasis cases reported in northwest Ohio' on August 4 confirming the continued decline in the daily rate. Lucas County is now tracking fewer than 10 new confirmed cases per day, down from daily increments exceeding 80 at the mid-July peak and 443 lab-positive cases during the peak week of July 5–11. The deceleration is consistent with post-boundary surveillance of the second unnamed cluster (93+ cases, food vehicle still unidentified by FDA under at least six parallel Cyclospora investigations) rather than any residual Taylor Farms exposure pathway. The August 5 TLCHD noon update is the next scheduled data point.
why_it_matters: The August 4 TLCHD update — 1,226 Lucas County cases, under 10 new cases per day — empirically confirms the primary Taco Bell/Taylor Farms outbreak is functionally concluded for the region. The only active open risk is the second unnamed cluster (93+ cases, food vehicle still unidentified by FDA). Michigan's first two deaths (August 3) are a national data point; both decedents had significant underlying health conditions and Lucas County health officials note cyclosporiasis deaths are rare in the U.S. Toledo's August calendar — Jeep Fest (August 6–9, 100K+ attendees) and Glass City JazzFest (August 14–15) — proceeds without any announced health-related changes. The outbreak's local public health chapter is at its conclusion phase; surveillance of the second cluster is the remaining watch-list item.
